lesson.title: The Electron Giveaway: What Oxidation Really Means
lesson.summary: Oxidation is the loss of electrons by an atom, ion, or molecule, which shows up in a formula as an increase in that atom's oxidation number.
lesson.body:
The word oxidation started out narrowly. Early chemists used it to describe a substance combining with oxygen, as when iron rusts or wood burns. That history is still worth knowing because it explains the name, but the modern definition is broader and more useful: oxidation is the loss of electrons, whether or not oxygen is anywhere in sight. Chemists remember the direction with a short mnemonic, OIL RIG: Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain, of electrons. Keep the first half of that phrase close, because the second half is coming in the next chapter.

You already know how to assign oxidation numbers to the atoms in a formula. That skill is exactly what lets you spot oxidation without watching electrons move in real time. If you track a particular atom across a reaction and its oxidation number goes up, that atom has been oxidized, full stop. It does not matter whether the electrons were fully transferred, as in an ionic compound, or just pulled toward a more electronegative neighbor, as in a covalent one. An increase in oxidation number is the signature oxidation leaves behind.

Consider magnesium metal reacting with oxygen gas to form magnesium oxide, a reaction you can watch as a strip of magnesium ribbon burns with a blinding white light. Focus just on the magnesium for now, written as a half reaction: Mg(s) is right arrow Mg2+ + 2e-. Before the reaction, magnesium metal has an oxidation number of 0, since it is an uncombined element. After the reaction, each magnesium atom exists as a Mg2+ ion, oxidation number +2. The number climbed from 0 to +2, an increase of 2, and the half reaction shows exactly why: each atom released two electrons, which appear on the product side. Losing 2 electrons per atom is precisely what raised the oxidation number by 2. The bookkeeping always matches.

One more thing worth noticing before you move on: those two electrons that magnesium gave up cannot simply disappear. Electrons are physical particles with mass and charge, not something a reaction can create or destroy. Every electron lost in an oxidation has to be picked up by something else in the same reaction, which is exactly the idea the next chapter builds on.
